A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MINJA research despite the changed title and formatting. The main text, mathematical notation, algorithms, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including figures containing image-only text.

before.justification: V1 reports original injection success, attack success, and utility results across four datasets, together with ablations and appendix analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and adds experiments on defenses, retrieval noise, model variants, utility loss, repeated testing, and progressive shortening.

M1.justification: MINJA retains the same bridging steps, indication prompts, progressive shortening, and storage of successful intermediate records. Section 4 and Algorithm 1 change notation and explanation, while Figure 2 rearranges the same prompts. The added PSS variants are evaluation ablations, not revisions to the proposed attack.

E1.justification: MIMIC-III, eICU, Webshop, MMLU, and the four victim-target categories remain unchanged. V3 adds actual malicious-query detection evaluation and a noisy-retrieval scenario within these domains. Additional model configurations do not introduce new dataset coverage, and proposed extensions to other agent types remain unevaluated.

E2.justification: V3 adds reduced-step and no-PSS reference variants in Table 12, and evaluates targeted versus general GPT-4o flagging defenses in Table 5. V1 only discussed moderation defenses. PANDORA's new Table 6 comparison is conceptual; it does not constitute an empirically evaluated competing attack.

E3.justification: New protocols include Gaussian retrieval noise with sigma 0.01, GPT-4o detection with benign false-positive controls, 2/5/8-demonstration and zero-shot QA evaluations, DeepSeek-R1 and Llama-2-7B configurations, and 18-query repeated tests. Section 5.1 also changes the stated EHRAgent/RAP retrieval counts from 3/4 to 4/3. This is a reported setting revision, without evidence establishing that the unchanged main results were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds retrieval-noise robustness, quantitative defense tests, MMLU utility analyses examining demonstration counts, query difficulty and embedding diversity, model-capability checks, within-pair stability tests, and PSS ablations. V1's attack-query diversity sweep in Table 3 is removed. Benign-record density, embedding-model, sequential-attack, and stepwise-ISR studies are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: V1 reports standard deviations across different victim-target pairs. V3 additionally reports three testing runs within fixed Pairs 1, 4, and 7 for RAP and QA with GPT-4/GPT-4o, using 18 sampled queries per run and replacement for QA (Appendix K, Table 11). This adds within-pair uncertainty reporting; it does not establish independent repetitions of the complete injection process or additional seeds.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical entries and the retained ablation results are unchanged. New results include DeepSeek-R1's 100% ISR and 90–100% ASR, retrieval-noise ASR of 95.6% versus 97.8% without noise, and full-PSS versus no-PSS ISR of 93.3% versus 75.6%. V3 also adds detection, utility, and repeated-test outcomes and removes the attack-query diversity results. These are additional condition-specific findings, not demonstrated across-version performance gains.

T1.justification: The victim-to-target formalization and progressive-shortening mathematics remain equivalent. Renaming attack-query notation and adding a conceptual PANDORA comparison do not introduce substantive mathematical results. Neither version contains theoretical theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claim that MINJA poisons agent memory through query-only interaction using bridging steps and progressive shortening. The three-agent evaluation and headline 98.2% injection success and 76.8% attack success remain unchanged. Reworked contribution bullets largely restate existing claims.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly identifies shared memory as an assumption and discusses identity disguise for isolated memory. It develops interpretations of defense detection versus false positives, within-pair versus between-pair variability, and weak-model evaluation. Appendix G strengthens the previously tentative benign-demonstration explanation of MMLU utility loss. Claims about several system defenses and alternative retrieval mechanisms remain argumentative rather than experimentally established.

D1.justification: V3 documents the GPT-4o judgment model and example detection prompts, and newly states API use and a future code release in its checklist and impact statement. This is additional reproducibility information, not evidence that code has become available. Existing attack prompts, victim-target lists, algorithm, and execution examples are substantially retained.

R1.justification: The positioning against AgentPoison and BadChain remains intact. Appendix F/Table 6 adds a focused conceptual distinction from PANDORA, while new citations support shared-memory assumptions, user feedback, and adversarial-training discussion. The Llama Guard citation is removed. These changes extend the positioning without fundamentally redefining it.

P1.justification: Beyond changing the title, v3 condenses the PSS explanation, rewrites and reorganizes the main-results discussion, moves continuous attacks into ablations as prior poisoning, and substantially rebuilds the defense discussion. The appendices are reorganized around additional analyses and positioning, with new acknowledgments, impact statements, and a checklist.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figure 1 adds a visual comparison with prior work, and Figure 2 changes from vertically stacked prompts to a two-by-two arrangement. New defense, conceptual-comparison, utility, model, stability, and PSS tables substantially expand the displays. Existing example and t-SNE figures are relocated, while the attack-query diversity table is removed.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses important validation gaps in v1: Table 5 quantifies defense detection and false positives where v1 offered discussion, while Appendices G, K, and L add utility controls, within-pair uncertainty, and direct evidence about PSS's contribution. These strengthen the empirical support for central mechanism and robustness arguments. The loss of the attack-query diversity sweep, unresolved setting-reporting ambiguities, and broad claims about untested defenses remain drawbacks, but the targeted validation gains provide a substantial net improvement.
